body.statement: The function \(G\mapsto|\mathcal I(G)|\), the number of independent sets of a finite simple graph, is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions.
body.proof_tex: Membership in \(\#\mathrm P\) is immediate: a vertex subset is a polynomial-size witness, and every edge can be checked in polynomial time. For hardness, start with an instance of Valiant's \(\mathrm{MONOTONE\ 2\mbox{-}SAT}\) problem. A clause of the form \(x_i\vee x_i\) forces \(x_i=1\); set every such variable to one and delete all clauses thereby satisfied. This preserves the number of satisfying assignments because each forced variable has exactly one possible value. Delete duplicate remaining clauses, and form the simple graph with one vertex per remaining variable and edge \(ij\) for the clause \(x_i\vee x_j\). A truth assignment satisfies all clauses exactly when its set of true variables is a vertex cover. Complementation is a bijection from vertex covers to independent sets, including arbitrary choices of isolated vertices. If preprocessing removes every variable, the answer is the directly computable value one; otherwise the graph is nonempty. Thus this is a polynomial-time count-preserving Turing reduction. Composing it with the cited \(\#\mathrm P\)-completeness of \(\mathrm{MONOTONE\ 2\mbox{-}SAT}\) proves \(\#\mathrm P\)-hardness under polynomial-time Turing reductions.
